subtitle: Sixteen merged pull requests from vLLM, Megatron-LM, and FastVideo replayed against running engines to compare traditional full-restart evaluation against live surgical patching and warm pre-forked recovery.

blocks.label: The cost of a plain restart

cases.b1: When a client submits a structured-output constraint that the engine backend cannot compile, vLLM's Python core raises a validation error, but the Rust frontend previously mapped all non-retryable engine failures to HTTP 500 internal server errors. This pull request updates `output.rs` and `error.rs` alongside the scheduler across ten files so that `RequestError` carries a validation error code that the HTTP server translates into a client-facing HTTP 400 response. By distinguishing malformed user constraints from internal crashes, the server gives callers accurate error codes without polluting server failure metrics.
cases.b2: Normally, testing a ten-file change spanning both the Python scheduler and the Rust frontend requires editing the source files and restarting the entire vLLM server from scratch. Even when weights and compiled artifacts are warm in caches, a plain restart takes 43 to 231 seconds across the replay because the process must repeat kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init before it can execute the check workload and the log-prob check. Without a live update mechanism, developers pay this multi-minute initialization tax on every edit-test iteration.
cases.b3: Because this change modifies STATE objects built once during startup—specifically constructor logic—FastRSI refuses an in-place live swap to avoid leaving initialized engine state inconsistent with the new class definitions. Instead of falling all the way back to a cold process launch, FastRSI restarts the engine from a warm pre-forked zygote copy that has already imported the runtime stack, completing the update in 16.6 seconds in eager mode and 51.2 seconds with CUDA graphs enabled. Although an earlier pass swapped the Python code in place in 0.38 seconds, enforcing clean state reconstruction via the pre-forked process guarantees safety while still cutting evaluation overhead.
cases.b4: In vLLM, an evaluation check runs the check workload followed by the log-prob check and counts as valid only if it confirms that the newly edited code actually executed during the test. For this replay, no check timing or output observation was recorded in the evaluation log. FastRSI also verifies reversibility by undoing the patch and returning the engine cleanly to its base state.

cases.b1: When vLLM initializes models with dummy weights for profiling or memory estimation, filling normalization layers with random values shrinks activations at every layer and distorts data-dependent kernels such as sparse top-k routing. This pull request updates `layernorm.py` to attach a `dummy_weight_value` attribute of `1.0` to multiplicative RMSNorm weights and `0.0` to zero-centered norm weights inside their `__init__` methods. Keeping normalization layers neutral during dummy initialization ensures that synthetic profiling passes trigger realistic kernel execution paths.
cases.b2: To evaluate this two-file change the traditional way, an engineer edits `layernorm.py` and restarts the vLLM process so the model loader rebuilds every layer from scratch. That plain restart takes 113 seconds in eager mode and 195 seconds when capturing CUDA graphs, because the engine must walk through kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init before running the check workload and the log-prob check. Paying over three minutes of startup overhead just to test a thirty-line change to dummy weight attributes makes rapid iteration painful.
cases.b3: This edit touches both STATE and NATIVE groups because it alters layer constructor attributes in `layernorm.py` that only take effect when model layers are instantiated. FastRSI therefore declines to patch the live process in place and instead launches from a warm pre-forked zygote that has already imported all dependencies, finishing in 9.2 seconds in eager mode and 44.9 seconds with CUDA graphs. Compared to the 113-second and 195-second plain restarts, recovering from the warm pre-forked copy eliminates most of the startup penalty while properly re-running layer construction.
cases.b4: A complete vLLM check requires executing the check workload and the log-prob check while verifying that the modified constructor paths actually ran during initialization. During an earlier attempt that tried to swap the code in place without rebuilding state, the modified constructors were never reached during the test step. With the warm pre-forked restart in place, the constructors run during model setup, though no separate check timing or output observation was recorded for this entry.

cases.b1: In vLLM's compilation pipeline, the `@eager_break_during_capture` decorator checked whether breakable CUDA graphs were enabled at module import time and immediately returned the unwrapped function if the flag was off. Because environment settings and compilation configs are often finalized after import, evaluating the check early in `breakable_cudagraph.py` prevented the wrapper from activating when needed at runtime. This pull request removes the import-time short-circuit so that the wrapper resolves the configuration dynamically at call time.
cases.b2: Evaluating a change to CUDA graph capture decorators normally forces a full process restart across all tensor-parallel workers. A plain vLLM restart must repeat kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init on every rank before executing the check workload and the log-prob check. Because decorator application happens when modules load and graphs are captured, there is no simple manual shortcut to test the edit without tearing down and rebuilding the serving engine.
cases.b3: This pull request touches GRAPH and RANKS, meaning the change affects code inside compiled or CUDA-graph-captured regions and must be applied consistently across all GPU ranks in a two-way tensor-parallel setup. Because the edit alters a decorator wrapping already-captured targets, FastRSI refuses a live in-place swap during the prepare phase and restarts the engine component instead. Refusing the live install prevents the ranks from committing a superficial function swap that would leave existing captured graphs running the old unbreakable code.
cases.b4: FastRSI counts a verification check only when it proves the edited code path actually ran during the test workload. When an earlier pass allowed a live swap across both tensor-parallel ranks, the check revealed that the newly swapped code never ran because the call sites remained bound to the previously captured targets. Refusing the live swap and restarting the component ensures the decorator is properly bound, although per-PR check timings and observations were not recorded.

cases.b1: When vLLM combines a thinking-token budget with speculative decoding, masked logits can take huge magnitudes that cause the split top-p Triton kernel in `topk_topp_triton.py` to suffer floating-point rounding errors. Converting the probability pivot back into logit space via `tl.log(pivot) + logZ + M` rounds the threshold directly to the maximum logit `M`, masking out every single token and forcing the sampler to emit token 0. This pull request fixes `_topp_sb_mask_kernel` to evaluate the keep predicate directly in probability space (`prob > pivot | (x == M)`), matching the step kernels bitwise.
cases.b2: Testing a bugfix inside a Triton sampling kernel ordinarily requires editing `topk_topp_triton.py` and restarting the vLLM server to recompile kernels and rebuild the execution graph. On a plain restart, the developer waits through kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init before the check workload and the log-prob check can test sampling behavior. Even for a localized 47-line edit, repeating full model initialization and graph capture dominates the debugging loop.
cases.b3: This edit modifies GRAPH code inside `topk_topp_triton.py`. In this replay, FastRSI did not install the change live and instead fell back to a restart because a plain Python function swap cannot recompile an already-JIT-compiled `@triton.jit` kernel in place. Support for rebuilding Triton kernels in place was added to FastRSI later and has not yet been re-run on this pull request.
cases.b4: Verification in vLLM runs the check workload and the log-prob check and confirms both output correctness and execution of the modified kernel. No per-PR check timing or output observation was recorded for this replay.

cases.b1: When many logits are already masked out before sampling—such as under structured decoding or sparse logit processors—the total number of finite logits in a row can be smaller than or equal to `k`. Previously, `_topk_topp_kernel` in `topk_topp_triton.py` still launched its binary search over outlier ranges to find a top-k cutoff even when every finite token was guaranteed to survive. This pull request short-circuits the search by setting `k_pivot = -inf` whenever `num_finite_total <= k`, and expands `benchmark_topk_topp.py` to measure sparse-input scenarios.
cases.b2: Without FastRSI, evaluating this performance optimization inside the sampler requires editing `topk_topp_triton.py` and restarting the vLLM engine if testing end-to-end serving, or re-running standalone benchmarks from cold imports. A full engine restart repeats kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init before running the check workload and the log-prob check. That heavy initialization cycle makes it slow to validate kernel tweaks inside a live serving pipeline.
cases.b3: Because the change modifies a `@triton.jit` kernel categorized under GRAPH in `topk_topp_triton.py`, swapping Python bytecode alone would leave the compiled GPU binary unchanged. FastRSI therefore fell back to a restart during this replay rather than installing the edit live. Native in-place Triton kernel rebuilding landed later and has not yet been replayed on this case.
cases.b4: A valid check on the running engine executes the check workload and the log-prob check while verifying that the updated Triton kernel actually ran. Specific check timings and observations were not recorded for this replay.

cases.b1: In vLLM's split top-p masking Triton kernel (`_topp_sb_mask_kernel` in `topk_topp_triton.py`), multiple tokens can share the exact boundary probability at the top-p cutoff. While the kernel computed a cumulative sum of tied elements within each block to keep only the required number of ties, it forgot to increment `num_preceding` by the block's tie count at the end of each loop iteration. This pull request adds the missing `num_preceding += tl.sum(dmask.to(tl.float32))` accumulation so boundary tie counts carry properly across blocks.
cases.b2: Testing this single-line fix in `topk_topp_triton.py` against a live vLLM server normally requires a full engine restart. The restart must step through kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init before executing the check workload and the log-prob check. Having to reload model weights and recapture CUDA graphs for a one-line kernel arithmetic fix illustrates how disproportionate standard evaluation overhead can be.
cases.b3: Like the other Triton sampler edits, this change touches GRAPH code inside a JIT-compiled Triton function in `topk_topp_triton.py`. Because swapping the Python function body in place could not trigger a Triton kernel rebuild at the time of the replay, FastRSI fell back to a restart. In-place Triton recompilation support was implemented later and has not yet been re-evaluated on this pull request.
cases.b4: Verifying the fix on the engine requires running the check workload and the log-prob check and confirming that the modified kernel executed during token sampling. No check timing or runtime observation was recorded in the replay log for this pull request.

cases.b1: vLLM's chunked prefill scheduler uses `long_prefill_token_threshold` to cap how many prompt tokens a long request can process in a single step so it does not starve concurrent requests of the token budget. However, `scheduler.py` previously enforced this cap even when only a single request was active in the entire batch, unnecessarily slicing a lone prompt across multiple scheduling steps. This pull request disables the threshold in `scheduler.py` and documents the behavior in `config/scheduler.py` whenever the total number of running and waiting requests is one.
cases.b2: Under a standard workflow, testing this scheduling logic requires editing `scheduler.py` and restarting the vLLM server from scratch. That plain restart takes 66.3 seconds because the engine must repeat kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init before running the check workload and the log-prob check. Even though the scheduler is pure Python host logic that does not touch GPU weights or kernels, a normal restart forces the developer to rebuild the entire GPU runtime.
cases.b3: Although the pull request updates a docstring on `SchedulerConfig` (STATE), the executable logic change in `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` sits inside the per-step `schedule` method (OP). FastRSI swaps the updated `schedule` function body directly into the live process between two engine steps in just 0.6 seconds. By patching the host-side Python method in place without disturbing loaded weights or captured CUDA graphs, FastRSI cuts the preparation time from 66.3 seconds to under a second.
cases.b4: To verify a scheduler patch in vLLM, the evaluation harness runs the check workload and the log-prob check and checks that the replaced `schedule` method was invoked during the run. No separate check timing or observation string was recorded for this entry.

cases.b1: In vLLM's Qwen GDN linear attention layer (`qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py`), merging speculative and non-speculative attention outputs previously allocated a temporary `merged_out` tensor, copied both subsets into it, and then copied the result into `core_attn_out`. That extra allocation and full-buffer copy added unnecessary memory traffic on every forward pass that mixed speculative and non-speculative tokens. This pull request eliminates the intermediate buffer in `_forward_core` and scatters both outputs directly into `core_attn_out` using in-place `index_copy_` calls.
cases.b2: Normally, evaluating this ten-line change in `qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py` requires stopping the server and performing a full vLLM restart. A plain restart takes 70.6 seconds as the engine repeats kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init prior to the check workload and the log-prob check. Because `_forward_core` executes inside the model's forward pass, there is no way to test the optimization on a live model without recapturing the affected execution graphs.
cases.b3: Because `_forward_core` in `qwen_gdn_linear_attn.py` is part of a GRAPH region, FastRSI swaps the Python function body in place and then selectively recaptures only the affected CUDA graphs between engine steps. The entire live install and selective graph recapture finishes in 2.4 seconds instead of the 70.6 seconds required for a plain restart. Skipping weight reloading and full engine initialization lets the developer measure forward-pass changes almost immediately.
cases.b4: Verification runs the check workload and the log-prob check against the patched engine and requires that the newly recaptured `_forward_core` path actually executed. No additional check timing or output observation was recorded in the log for this case.

cases.b1: Several model architectures in vLLM—such as `apertus.py` and `deepseek_v2.py`—apply RMSNorm to query and key projections right after splitting a fused QKV tensor along its last dimension. Because `fused_add_rms_norm_kernel` in `layernorm_kernels.cu` previously required contiguous residual tensors, those models had to materialize `.contiguous()` copies before normalizing, hurting performance. This pull request adds an explicit `residual_stride` parameter to the CUDA kernel and removes the redundant `.contiguous()` calls across model definitions for a 1.2x to 3.1x kernel speedup.
cases.b2: Testing a change that spans both C++/CUDA kernel source (`layernorm_kernels.cu`) and Python model definitions normally means recompiling the extension and restarting the vLLM engine. A plain restart must run through kernel autotune, weight load, CUDA graph capture, and engine init before executing the check workload and the log-prob check. Rebuilding native extensions and reloading multi-gigabyte model weights makes iterative CUDA kernel tuning especially slow.
cases.b3: Because this pull request modifies NATIVE C++/CUDA source in `layernorm_kernels.cu`, FastRSI compiles the updated kernel into a versioned side shared library, rebinds the Python operator to the new symbol, and recaptures the affected graphs inside the running process. Installing the native edit live takes 28 seconds, completely avoiding a process restart and model weight reload. Once bound, the running engine immediately dispatches normalization calls to the newly compiled CUDA kernel.
cases.b4: After rebinding the native library, vLLM verification runs the check workload and the log-prob check to confirm numerical accuracy and ensure the new kernel symbol ran. Plain-restart timing and check observation details were not recorded for this case.

cases.b1: When Megatron-LM trains with low-precision gradient communication buffers, scaling gradients by a Python `float` token-scaling factor can cause precision loss or type promotion issues during distributed data-parallel synchronization. This pull request updates `scale_gradients` across six files—including `distributed_data_parallel.py` and `param_and_grad_buffer.py`—to pass and maintain the scaling factor as an FP32 `torch.Tensor`. Keeping the factor in 32-bit floating point preserves numerical accuracy when scaling low-precision gradient buckets.
cases.b2: In a standard Megatron-LM workflow, testing an edit across six distributed training modules requires terminating the job and launching a fresh multi-GPU training run. A plain restart takes 79 to 89 seconds because the training engine must execute start-up, CUDA graph capture, the first step, warm-up, and the warm-up protocol before the check workload can run a single test step. Repeating distributed initialization and warmup steps for every small code change severely slows down training development.
cases.b3: The modified `scale_gradients` methods in `distributed_data_parallel.py` and `param_and_grad_buffer.py` are per-call Python functions (OP). FastRSI swaps the updated function bodies across all three affected runtime modules directly in place in 0.18 seconds between training steps. Avoiding the 79-to-89-second restart lets the training job continue immediately from its warm state.
cases.b4: FastRSI ran a four-step training check and observed a loss within 4.4e-5 of the base run, but execution tracking showed that none of the three patched `scale_gradients` methods were ever called. Because the test workload uses bf16 gradient buffers, it never enters the low-precision buffer scaling code path that this pull request modifies. Under FastRSI's verification rule, a check counts only if the edited code actually ran, so FastRSI flags that this workload cannot exercise the patch despite the fast install.

cases.b1: During a Megatron-LM training run, `get_start_time_from_progress_log` in `megatron/training/training.py` repeatedly opens and parses `progress.txt` on the shared filesystem to read the job's initial start timestamp and completed FLOP count. Because those values never change once a run has started, re-reading the file on every logging or checkpoint interval wastes filesystem I/O. This pull request splits the helper in `training.py` and decorates `_get_start_time_from_progress_log` with `@functools.cache` keyed on the save directory and world size.
cases.b2: Normally, trying out this nineteen-line change in `training.py` requires stopping the training job and restarting Megatron-LM from the beginning. That plain restart costs 79 to 89 seconds while the engine steps through start-up, CUDA graph capture, the first step, warm-up, and the warm-up protocol ahead of the check workload. Waiting nearly a minute and a half of cluster time just to test a `@functools.cache` decorator makes quick cleanup patches expensive to verify.
cases.b3: Because `get_start_time_from_progress_log` in `training.py` is a standard Python function (OP), FastRSI installs the new cached helper and updated function body in place in 0.37 seconds. The live swap completes between two training steps without interrupting the distributed process group or reloading model state. That cuts the wait before running the check from 79–89 seconds down to a fraction of a second.
cases.b4: To verify the edit, FastRSI executed a four-step training check and confirmed the training loss remained within 1.5e-4 of the baseline. However, runtime call tracking showed that `get_start_time_from_progress_log` was never invoked during those four steady-state steps because it is startup-only code. Because a check counts only when the edited code actually executes, FastRSI reports that an in-flight step check between steady-state iterations never reaches this startup path.

cases.b1: When initializing `DistributedDataParallel` in `distributed_data_parallel.py`, Megatron-LM asserts that the per-bucket gradient scaling factor divided by the data-parallel group size equals the target scaling factor. Using exact floating-point equality (`==`) in `__init__` caused spurious assertion failures whenever `scaling_factor / data_parallel_group.size()` produced minor IEEE-754 rounding differences. This pull request replaces the exact equality check with `math.isclose(..., rel_tol=1e-9)` so valid scaling factors pass initialization.
cases.b2: Testing an assertion inside `DistributedDataParallel.__init__` normally requires editing `distributed_data_parallel.py` and restarting the Megatron-LM training run. A full restart must run through start-up, CUDA graph capture, the first step, warm-up, and the warm-up protocol before reaching the check workload. Because DDP initialization happens once when wrapping the model at startup, simply swapping the method on an already-running trainer would never test the assertion.
cases.b3: This edit touches both OP and STATE because it modifies the `__init__` constructor of `DistributedDataParallel` in `distributed_data_parallel.py`. FastRSI detects the constructor edit and refuses the live install in 0.07 seconds rather than performing a misleading in-place swap that would skip constructor execution. It then falls back to a restart that brings the training engine back to ready in 88.8 seconds (and also tested a warm pre-forked zygote path, which took 148.7 seconds on a first fork with an unexplained slow warmup).
cases.b4: Because the engine restarted to run the modified `DistributedDataParallel.__init__` constructor, the updated `math.isclose` assertion executed during setup as required. FastRSI then ran an eight-step verification check (the check workload) and confirmed the training run completed with no regression, keeping the loss within 1.0e-3 and the gradient norm within 2.6e-3 of the baseline.

cases.b1: Megatron-LM's fine-grained activation offloading overlaps CPU-to-GPU activation reloads with backward computation, but partial offloading had bugs in how warmup bookkeeping, margin offload groups, and non-contiguous QKV views were handled. This pull request makes an extensive 933-line change across eight files—including `fine_grained_activation_offload.py` and `attention.py`—to add `is_offload_margin` and `_offload_info_collected` state fields, refine reload event synchronization, and check QKV tensor storage aliasing before core attention. Together, these changes prevent corrupted activations and deadlocks during warmup and backward passes.
cases.b2: Evaluating a 933-line change across eight core pipeline and transformer files normally requires a full Megatron-LM process restart. That restart must repeat start-up, CUDA graph capture, the first step, warm-up, and the warm-up protocol before the check workload can test the training loop. When iterating on complex activation offloading logic, waiting through full process startup and warmup after every edit slows debugging considerably.
cases.b3: Because this pull request modifies OP and STATE—including constructor edits, new instance fields in `fine_grained_activation_offload.py`, and a removed method definition—FastRSI refuses an in-place live install in 0.60 seconds. Instead of starting from a cold Python process, FastRSI restarts the engine from a warm pre-forked zygote that has already imported the framework, reaching a ready state in 40.9 seconds compared to 78.8 seconds for a full code restart. Refusing the unsafe live patch while recovering from the pre-forked zygote nearly halves the restart time and still reconstructs all offload state cleanly.
cases.b4: After rebuilding the engine from the warm pre-forked copy, FastRSI verified the patch with an eight-step training check. The check confirmed that the modified initialization and attention forward paths ran without regression, producing a training loss within 1.5e-3 of the baseline and a gradient norm within 3.9e-3.

cases.b1: In FastVideo's MiniMax-H3 pipeline, encoding reference keyframes for conditioning in `minimax_h3_latent_preparation.py` previously called `self.vae.to(vae_device)` directly, ignoring the host-weight cache managed by the video VAE offload system. That redundant transfer bypassed pinned CPU memory optimizations and reloaded VAE weights unnecessarily during conditioning. This pull request updates `_encode_fl2va_conditions` to load the VAE onto the target device via `pinned_offload.load(self.vae, vae_device, pin=fastvideo_args.pin_cpu_memory)` so keyframe encoding reuses the cached host weights.
cases.b2: Under a normal workflow, testing this 225-line change in `minimax_h3_latent_preparation.py` requires killing the FastVideo process and starting a fresh run. A warm plain restart takes 107 seconds from launch to the completion of the first generated video because the engine must repeat imports and init, weight load, the JIT build, and start-up before executing the check workload. Reloading multi-gigabyte diffusion and VAE weights just to test a stage helper method turns a quick check into a nearly two-minute wait.
cases.b3: Because the edit in `minimax_h3_latent_preparation.py` touches only per-call Python stage functions (OP), FastRSI swaps the updated function bodies in place in 0.086 seconds, with a total edit-to-run time of 0.81 seconds. The live engine keeps all diffusion weights, JIT-compiled kernels, and pipeline state resident in GPU memory. Generation proceeds immediately, taking 6.00 seconds for the edited video compared to 107 seconds for a full restart.
cases.b4: FastRSI generated one video before the edit (6.10 seconds), one with the edit installed (6.00 seconds), and one after undoing the edit (6.01 seconds), confirming bit-exact output across all three runs. However, runtime call tracking showed that the modified keyframe encoding code was never reached because the test workload runs text-to-video generation without reference keyframes. Because a verification check counts only when the changed code actually runs, FastRSI explicitly reports that this text-to-video workload cannot exercise or measure the keyframe conditioning optimization.

cases.b1: During Video Sparse Attention (VSA) inference in FastVideo, preprocessing queries, keys, and values into tiled `BHSD` layout previously required scattering tiles into an intermediate `BSHD` buffer followed by four separate `BSHD`-to-`BHSD` transpose kernels. This pull request adds a fused Triton kernel (`_tile_to_bhsd_kernel` in `vsa_tile_layout.py`) and updates `video_sparse_attn.py` so SM100 GPUs write tiled `BHSD` tensors directly in a single pass. Fusing the scatter and layout transpose eliminates intermediate memory reads and writes during sparse attention preprocessing.
cases.b2: Normally, evaluating this nine-file change across `vsa_tile_layout.py`, `video_sparse_attn.py`, and `envs.py` requires a full FastVideo restart. A plain restart takes 107 seconds as the process repeats imports and init, weight load, the JIT build, and start-up before running the check workload to generate a test video. Re-running heavy model weight loading and JIT compilation makes it slow to validate whether pipeline changes affect end-to-end generation.
cases.b3: Because this pull request touches OP, STATE, and module-level definitions (`restart`)—including a removed definition and changes outside hot-swappable functions in `envs.py`—FastRSI refuses a live in-place install in 0.20 seconds. It then falls back to launching the check in a warm new process, where generating the test video takes 6.19 seconds once initialized, compared to 107 seconds for a full plain restart from scratch. Refusing the live swap prevents partial module updates when top-level environment definitions and new kernel modules are added.
cases.b4: Verification generated a warm test video in 6.19 seconds and confirmed that the output was bit-exact with the baseline. At the same time, inspection showed that the MiniMax-H3 test workload does not use the generic VSA attention backend modified by this pull request, so the new SM100 tile layout path had no effect on this workload.

cases.b1: Decoding video latents in FastVideo's MiniMax-H3 VAE splits frames into spatial tiles, and `FASTVIDEO_H3_VAE_TILE_BATCH` in `envs.py` previously defaulted to `1`, decoding only a single spatial tile per ViT decoder call. Because the ViT decoder treats batch entries independently (except on NVFP4 decoders with dynamic activation scales), decoding one tile at a time underutilized the GPU. This pull request raises the default in `envs.py` to `8` tiles per call and updates `minimax_h3_video.py` and `minimax_h3_parallel.py`, significantly speeding up high-resolution VAE decoding.
cases.b2: Testing a seven-file change touching `envs.py` and the MiniMax-H3 VAE modules (`minimax_h3_video.py` and `minimax_h3_parallel.py`) normally requires restarting the FastVideo process. A plain restart takes 86 seconds because the engine must go through imports and init, weight load, the JIT build, and start-up before executing the check workload. Waiting 86 seconds to reload model weights just to test a default batch-size change slows down configuration and pipeline tuning.
cases.b3: Although part of the diff touches per-call methods (OP), it also modifies `FASTVIDEO_H3_VAE_TILE_BATCH` at module level in `envs.py` (`restart`). FastRSI detects these module-level changes outside hot-swappable functions, refuses the live in-place install in 0.18 seconds, and runs the evaluation in a warm new process where the test video completes in 6.13 seconds. Refusing the in-place swap ensures that module-level environment defaults are properly re-evaluated rather than silently ignored.
cases.b4: The verification check generated a warm video in 6.13 seconds and confirmed that the output remained bit-exact with the baseline. However, because this evaluation workload explicitly configures the tile batch size to 12, changing the fallback default in `envs.py` from 1 to 8 does not alter the runtime behavior on this test workload.

_about: Case-study wording written by Gemini (gemini-4-argon-medium) on 2026-11-14 from prs.json records and the upstream diffs; pasted as returned, with phase ids spelled as words.
